tier_reason: The independent ProgrammerAL/SerializationBenchmarks repo publishes its BenchmarkDotNet code against Google.Protobuf and MessagePack-CSharp: Benchmarks/Deserialize_Once_ComplexPocos.cs and 17 sibling classes, run by Benchmarks/Program.cs, with the schemas in SerializationEntities/. Each results page states the toolchain (.NET SDK 6.0.100-preview.7, .NET 5.0.9 X64 RyuJIT, BenchmarkDotNet 0.13.1 DefaultJob, which builds in Release) and the CPU (AMD Ryzen 9 3950X), so it is A, the same call as the earlier Sep and simdunicode BenchmarkDotNet entries.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Deserialize complex POCO once, mean latency: BebopStruct 166.1 ns vs Protobuf (Google.Protobuf, C#) 1,051.4 ns (~6.3x) and vs MessagePack-CSharp 1,584.6 ns (~9.5x). BebopMessage 231.7 ns is ~4.5x faster than Protobuf and ~6.8x faster than MessagePack (ratios derived from page data). The benchmark repo's README says Bebop is 'the fastest in every benchmark, serialization and deserialization', and that on deserialization Protobuf 'becomes the slowest of the binary serializers'.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: BenchmarkDotNet v0.13.1 DefaultJob (default Release build configuration, X64 RyuJIT), .NET SDK 6.0.100-preview.7.21379.14, runtime .NET 5.0.9 (5.0.921.35908). The net5.0 target sets no custom optimization properties in Benchmarks/Benchmarks.csproj. Packages: bebop 2.2.6, Google.Protobuf 3.17.3, MessagePack 2.3.75.
corrections.hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3950X, 1 CPU, 32 logical and 16 physical cores. BenchmarkDotNet reports the OS as Windows 10.0.22449.
corrections.caveats: All numbers are C#: Bebop 2.2.6 vs the C# Protobuf (Google.Protobuf 3.17.3) and MessagePack-CSharp 2.3.75 runtimes on .NET 5.0.9, run in 2021. Bebop is now at v3.2.3 (2025-09-16) and .NET 5 is out of support, so current versions are untested. The benchmark repo is small (6 stars, last commit 2021-09-05) and publishes a single BenchmarkDotNet run on one desktop. The complex-POCO schemas are not like-for-like, which inflates Protobuf's complex-deserialize cost: Protobuf stores the child GUID as a string and uses google.protobuf.Timestamp sub-messages and double Percentage/Cost, Bebop uses native guid/date/float32, and MessagePack uses a decimal Cost. On the like-for-like tiny POCO (two int32 fields), Deserialize_Once_TinyPocos still shows BebopStruct 11.93 ns vs Protobuf 85.51 ns (~7.2x, derived). Serialization gains are much smaller, e.g. Serialize_Once_SimplePocos BebopMessage 94.40 ns vs Protobuf 100.82 ns (~1.07x) and Serialize_Once_ComplexPocos BebopStruct 239.2 ns vs Protobuf 926.5 ns (~3.9x) (derived). Bebop's serialize allocates more than both baselines: 1,032 B for complex serialize-once BebopStruct vs 400 B for Protobuf and 304 B for MessagePack. Bebop's own README claims ~10x over Protobuf in C# and TypeScript, but shows only a chart image.

notes: All six rows in the record match the page, and Bebop leads in all 18 BenchmarkResults tables. I pointed benchmark_url at the canonical /blob/main/ path (/blob/master/ 302-redirects to it) and set compared_against_cpp_std_directly to false, because the baselines are C# Protobuf/MessagePack runtimes, not the C++ standard library. The 6.3x complex figure is flattered by a schema mismatch (see caveats), but the like-for-like tiny-POCO table still shows ~7x, so the tier stays A.

tier_reason: The wire-size and allocation tables in docs/COMPETITIVE.md come from the public bench/ module (bench/memory_compare_test.go TestMemoryReport, bench/protobuf_bench_test.go, bench/competitor.go), run by scripts/compare.sh with `go test -bench -benchmem -count=6` on a default build. The page states Go 1.26 (docs/BENCH.md: Go 1.26.0) and an Intel i7-9750H, so the size claim against Protobuf, FlatBuffers and msgpack is A. The Active-Directory json/msgpack speed rows are weaker (see caveats).

corrections.baseline: Protocol Buffers, FlatBuffers, MessagePack (wire size); MessagePack and Go encoding/json (encode/decode speed)
corrections.claimed_speedup: Wire size at the qdf_compression tier vs protobuf on 5 batch fixtures: RTB 203,360 vs 327,700 B (-38%), IoT 148,177 vs 207,562 B (-29%), OTLP 179,181 vs 561,860 B (-68%), Logs 62,149 vs 156,479 B (-60%), Events 39,639 vs 64,978 B (-39%), i.e. up to 68% smaller than Protobuf. On a 5,000-user Active-Directory export, qdf OptBalanced gives 1,830 KB, 6.6 ms encode and 7.9 ms decode, against encoding/json at 3,833 KB / 14.1 ms / 57.8 ms and msgpack at 3,370 KB / 8.7 ms / 16.7 ms. The page's summary: 2.1x smaller and 2.1x faster encode than json, ~7x faster decode than json, and 1.8x smaller with ~2x faster decode than msgpack. qdf is not faster than protobuf or FlatBuffers. Per the page, protobuf and FlatBuffers win raw decode throughput and FlatBuffers wins encode allocation outright. Protobuf wins single-tiny-message size and max encode throughput. qdf_balanced and qdf_compression do not win on allocation, though qdf_speed allocates less than protobuf on 4 of 5 fixtures.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Go 1.26 gc toolchain (docs/BENCH.md: Go 1.26.0), default build. scripts/compare.sh runs `go test -run='^$' -bench='RTB|IoT|OTLP|Logs|Events' -benchmem -count=6` in bench/ plus `EMIT_MEM=1 go test -run=TestMemoryReport`. go.mod and bench/go.mod now require go 1.27.0, so the published 2026-06-01 numbers predate the current modules.
corrections.caveats: The project is alpha and pre-1.0, and its wire format is still changing. It has 26 stars and was created 2026-05-24. Against Protobuf the win is wire size, not speed: the page concedes that protobuf and FlatBuffers win raw decode throughput. Speed numbers come from a single i7-9750H laptop run dated 2026-06-01 on Go 1.26, and the author notes they are machine-specific. The AD-export encoding/json and msgpack timings have no public harness for the competitor side, because bench/realistic_ad_test.go and bench/realistic_ad_bench_test.go time only qdf. The README now quotes different figures: ≈6x faster decode than JSON and ~1.5x faster than msgpack on AD, and -24 to -77% wire vs protobuf on GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest. Reproducible qdf vs msgpack/json speed tables are in docs/BENCH.md (bench/profiles_test.go, Go 1.26.0, i7-9750H). qdf_compression encode is slow, about 70 MB/s on the IoT float batch.

notes: Every figure in the record appears in docs/COMPETITIVE.md. I made four corrections. The record credited single-tiny-message size to FlatBuffers, but the page gives it to protobuf. I narrowed baseline so the speed wins are only against msgpack and encoding/json. I set compared_against_cpp_std_directly to false. I set last_commit to the HEAD committer date, 2026-09-18 (author date 2026-09-01).

tier_reason: The README's 'Performance & footprint' section compares generated Quarry C/C++ with protoc-generated Protobuf C++, both default and Arena. It uses the public harness in benchmarks/c/proof_benchmark.c, benchmarks/cpp/proof_benchmark.cpp and benchmarks/protobuf/proof_benchmark.cpp, driven by benchmarks/scripts/run_benchmarks.py. The README states GCC 13.3.0, a Release build and an AMD EPYC 7763; the CI manifest confirms the compiler, CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release and libprotoc 3.21.12. Code, compiler, flags and CPU are all present, so A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Results are mixed. The README table is from commit 04349e57, medians of 5 CI runs, in ops/s. Protobuf C++ wins telemetry encode (18.81M vs Quarry C 9.69M), telemetry decode (13.48M vs 5.45M) and large encode (1.60M vs 0.48M). Quarry C wins large decode: 0.85M vs 0.57M for Protobuf C++ (~1.5x) and 0.45M for Protobuf Arena (~1.9x). It also beats Protobuf Arena on large encode, 0.48M vs 0.37M (~1.3x) (ratios derived from page data). Quarry C++ is slower than Protobuf C++ in every row. BRF is larger on the wire: 60 vs 16 bytes/record for telemetry and 1,661 vs 1,425 for large.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.3.0 (`c++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0`), CMake preset docker-benchmark with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (CMake's GCC Release default: -O3 -DNDEBUG). The project builds as C++20 and the Quarry C harness as C99, in an Ubuntu 24.04 dev container. Protobuf/protoc 3.21.12 (libprotoc 3.21.12).
corrections.hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 64-Core Processor, Linux x86_64, GitHub-hosted runner (docker compose dev container)
corrections.caveats: The project has 4 stars and a single maintainer. It was created 2026-06-19 and is pre-1.0 (v0.1.30-rc.3). The author says the suite 'does not rank backends' and calls the ownership differences 'not a backend-quality ranking'. Quarry C decodes into a caller-owned fixed-capacity struct with no heap allocation, while Protobuf C++ allocates a fresh owning message per decode, so the large-decode win mostly reflects the API model. Shared GitHub-hosted runners add noise. Protobuf 3.21.12 is the Ubuntu distro build, not current Protobuf. Numbers move between commits. The CI artifact for HEAD 5c8adcde (2026-09-20) has Quarry C ahead of Protobuf C++ on large decode (1.17M vs 0.574M ops/s, ~2.0x), nested decode (2.84M vs 1.76M, ~1.6x), large round-trip (~1.6x), nested round-trip (~1.3x) and configuration encode (~1.09x). The same artifact has it behind on telemetry, stress, configuration decode and large/nested encode (ratios derived from artifact data). CI artifacts expire, so the README table is the stable reference.

notes: The README table matches the record exactly. The case is borderline because Protobuf wins most rows and the author makes no speed claim. I kept it rather than rejecting as not-faster: Quarry C is measurably faster than Protobuf C++ on large-payload decode in both the README baseline and the latest CI run, which also shows a nested-decode win, and the record reports this honestly. I set compared_against_cpp_std_directly to false and added the compiler and flag provenance from the CI manifest.
